marble.name: Weather vs climate
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions of the world, distinguishing between weather and climate
marble.prompt: Can you explain the difference between weather and climate, and describe why the Arctic is always cold while tropical areas are always warm?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning to observe and describe weather patterns and seasons, while exploring how plants and animals change their environment to meet their needs.

misconceptions: 'Weather and climate are the same thing' — treating today's weather as the region's climate.
'One unusual day changes the climate' — e.g. a freak snowfall means the desert now has a cold climate.
'Climate = temperature only' — ignoring rainfall, wind, seasonality that also define a climate.
'Cold/warmer weather today disproves or proves climate change' — conflating a single reading with a long-term trend.
'Places have one fixed weather' — not seeing that weather varies day to day while the climate pattern stays stable.
representations: A timescale slider/zoom: today → this week → this season → many years, watching day-to-day variation average out.
Climate-zone world map (tap a region to see its typical climate profile).
Climate graphs / climographs — average monthly temperature and rainfall bars for a region.
Two-region side-by-side data tables of daily weather turning into typical-condition summaries.
authoredAnswer: The friend is wrong. A single cold week is weather — what the atmosphere does day to day. Climate is the typical pattern of weather averaged over many years, so one cold spell doesn't show the climate is changing; you'd need decades of data.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Yes — a colder week means London's climate is getting colder.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Cites one short event as proof about climate; treats today's weather as a climate trend.
wrongAnswers.fix: Confront it — show a 30-year temperature record and ask how many years make a climate; contrast one point with the average.

wrongAnswers.wrong: No — because climate is the weather across a whole big region, and one city is too small to count.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Separates weather and climate by how much area they cover rather than by time span.
wrongAnswers.fix: Contrast a single day's weather map (weather) with a 30-year average for the same place (climate).

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Explains why tropical regions have a hot climate by closeness to the sun.
wrongAnswers.fix: Use a globe and a torch to show the angle of sunlight at the equator vs poles; distance to the sun is essentially the same.
